column4: The section presents 87:6 as Allah causing the Prophet to read. Here the same address restrains his tongue from hurrying to receive the recitation, giving the preservation promise its immediate setting.

The section's dictionary form قرأت الشيء defines reading as gathering parts together. Here Allah says, “عَلَيْنَا جَمْعَهُ وَقُرْآنَهُ,” making gathering and recitation the divine work behind the promise.

The section's dictionary describes reading as joining words in recitation. This verse says that once Allah recites it, the Prophet is to follow that recitation; it spells out how the received words are held.

This follows the collection, recitation, and following in 75:17–18 with “ثُمَّ إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا بَيَانَهُ.” Its contribution is the completing explanation of the recited revelation, not a further claim about memorization.
The section itself cites this command to the Prophet not to hurry with the Quran before its revelation is completed. It joins the Quran's arrival to the section's promise of recitation and retention.

The section's dictionary form القراءة defines reading as joining letters and words in ترتيل. This verse explicitly commands “وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا,” giving that manner of measured recitation a Quranic formulation.
The section's dictionary form قرأت الشيء means gathering parts together. Here the Quran is divided for people to be recited “عَلَى مُكْثٍ,” linking collected revelation to its gradual public reading.

The objection asks why the Quran was not sent down all at once; the answer says it was sent thus to strengthen the Prophet's heart and recited in order. That adds why a gathered, paced revelation supports retention.

The section's dictionary form أقرأت غيري means causing another to read. Here Allah's command “اقْرَأْ” addresses a human reader directly, a close counterpart to the Prophet being made to recite in 87:6.

The section names reading as the joining of words and 87:6 as causing another to read. The repeated “اقْرَأْ” is likewise a divine command to the Prophet to read, now paired with the Lord's generosity.

The section's dictionary form قرأت الشيء defines reading as joining words together. This verse says the people given the Book recite it as it should be recited and believe in it, linking faithful reading with receiving scripture.

The section's image asks how a recited word is gathered and retained. This verse says to listen and be quiet when the Quran is recited, giving the hearer's attentive reception as a counterpart to the Prophet's paced recitation.
The section describes suhuf as material pieces on which writing is made. “الَّذِي عَلَّمَ بِالْقَلَمِ” gives the writing tool behind such pages and connects the recited word to inscription.

The section connects the recited word and written scripture with purification. Abraham asks for a messenger who recites God's signs, teaches the Book and wisdom, and purifies the people, bringing those same acts together in one request.

The section notes how purified pages hold a reminder. This verse joins the Messenger's reciting God's signs, purifying people, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, giving a direct meeting of recitation, purification, and scripture.

This repeats the pairing in 3:164: the Messenger recites signs, purifies people, and teaches the Book. It directly connects recitation and purification, the two qualities the section brings together through the elevated and purified pages.

The section's image moves from words held in memory to words written on pages. “عَلَّمَ الْإِنْسَانَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ” adds the knowledge conveyed and retained through that teaching, though the verse does not itself mention a page.
The section says that prophetic books are ذكر and that suhuf are written sheets. This verse brings both together: a Messenger recites “صُحُفًا مُطَهَّرَةً” containing valuable writings.

The section's dictionary form التذكرة is something by which a need is recalled. “إِنَّهَا تَذْكِرَةٌ” calls the revelation itself a reminder, directly connecting the instrument of recall to the scripture.
The section distinguishes the reminder from the act of remembering it. “فَمَنْ شَاءَ ذَكَرَهُ” makes that response voluntary, as 87:9–10 distinguishes the reminder from the person who remembers.
The section's dictionary defines suhuf as written sheets and explains that earlier scripture is on such pages. This verse locates the reminder “فِي صُحُفٍ مُكَرَّمَةٍ.”
The section's page image is writing preserved on sheets. Here the pages are “مَرْفُوعَةٍ مُطَهَّرَةٍ,” adding their elevated and purified status to the reminder carried in them.

This continues the pages of 80:13–14 by saying they are in the hands of scribes. The added detail identifies the bearers who write or transmit the page, rather than merely repeating its material form.
This completes the scribe description begun in 80:15: the scribes are noble and righteous. It adds the character of those who handle the pages named in the preceding ayat.

The section links written pages with a تذكرة that brings a needed matter back to mind. In the debt-writing instructions, witnesses are chosen so that if one errs, “فَتُذَكِّرَ إِحْدَاهُمَا الْأُخْرَى”; writing and mutual reminding protect a detail from being lost.

The section defines a sahifa as a written piece of leather or parchment. The oath “وَكِتَابٍ مَسْطُورٍ فِي رَقٍّ مَنْشُورٍ” explicitly places writing on spread parchment, a material parallel to the section's pages.

The section describes written pages gathered as scripture. This verse speaks of making the Book into sheets, then “يُبْدُونَهَا وَيُخْفُونَ كَثِيرًا”; it adds the boundary between what is exposed and what is hidden in a written revelation.

The section's suhuf are pieces bearing writing. This verse imagines a Book sent down on parchment that people touch with their hands, then records their response that it is manifest magic; the physical page does not guarantee acceptance of its message.
The section connects recitation and memory to a written scripture. This verse calls the Quran “كَرِيمٌ,” introducing the revelation described in the following ayat as a noble Quran.
The section says a mushaf gathers written pages into a book. Here the Quran is “فِي كِتَابٍ مَكْنُونٍ,” explicitly joining recited revelation to a kept book.
This follows the hidden book of 56:78 with a statement about who may touch it. It adds a boundary around access to the written record, which the section's page-and-book image leaves implicit.

This completes the description in 56:77–79 by calling the Quran a sending-down from the Lord of the worlds. Its contribution identifies the source of the book whose preservation and handling the preceding ayat describe.
The section links the prophet's spoken reminder to written pages. “بَلْ هُوَ قُرْآنٌ مَجِيدٌ” names the Quran as the revelation whose written preservation is specified in the next ayah.
This completes 85:21 by locating that Quran “فِي لَوْحٍ مَحْفُوظٍ.” It gives the section's retained-and-written word an explicit preserved-record counterpart.
The section's dictionary form النسيان is the opposite of remembering and preserving. Allah calls the revelation “الذِّكْرَ” and says He guards it, joining reminder to preservation directly.

The section joins remembering with reciting and retaining scripture. This verse asks how people can command righteousness while forgetting themselves even as they recite the Book, bringing reading and failure to remember into one rebuke.

The section's dictionary form النسيان includes leaving something behind. Here the Messenger complains that his people have taken the Quran as “مَهْجُورًا,” abandoned; it makes neglect of the revealed word explicit.

The section connects the first pages with the choice to prefer worldly life. This verse describes heirs of the Book taking the fleeting world's goods, though they studied its contents; it then says the Hereafter is better, bringing scripture reception and worldly preference together in one scene.

This follows 7:169's heirs who take worldly gain despite their Book by praising those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer. It supplies the contrasting response of keeping the scripture's instruction.

The section's dictionary says that the books of the prophets are ذكر. This verse calls the revelation “ذِكْرٌ مُّبَارَكٌ” and says it was sent down, directly joining a prophetic book to the section's reminder sense.

The section's dictionary form الذكر includes a book containing the religion's details. This verse calls the revelation a reminder for the Prophet and his people and says they will be questioned about it, connecting scripture with an address that is retained and answered.
The section links the reminder to written pages and a collected book. This verse calls the Reminder a mighty Book when it comes to people, explicitly joining those two forms of revelation.
This continues the mighty Book in 41:41 by saying falsehood cannot approach it from before or behind. It adds a claim of protection to the section's image of a word preserved in pages.

Pharaoh asks Moses about “الْقُرُونِ الْأُولَى,” the earlier generations. The section's dictionary form الأُولى means the beginning or earliest part; Moses' answer in 20:52 then connects those generations with a book held by God.

The section itself cites Moses' answer: their knowledge is with his Lord in a book, and his Lord neither strays nor forgets. This directly joins a written record of the earlier generations to divine non-forgetting.

The section's dictionary form النسيان is what is opposite to remembrance and keeping. In its own context the angels say, “وَمَا كَانَ رَبُّكَ نَسِيًّا,” a compact parallel to the Lord who does not forget in 20:52.

The section itself cites the question whether the people have received proof of what is in the earlier pages. This ayah directly connects the dictionary's “earliest” pages with evidence presented to an audience.

The section itself cites “وَإِنَّهُ لَفِي زُبُرِ الْأَوَّلِينَ.” Its claim that the Quran is in the books of earlier peoples joins the recited revelation to the section's dictionary sense of the first writings.

The section says the earlier pages contain the message and quotes this opening question about what is in Moses' pages. This verse directly names those pages as the source of the teachings that follow.
The section identifies the earlier pages with Ibrahim and Moses. This verse names Ibrahim and says he fulfilled his charge, beginning the specific contents of the pages introduced in 53:36.
The section cites the first teaching from the pages: no burden-bearer bears another's burden. This verse is that teaching, giving the remembered scripture a rule of individual responsibility.

The section quotes the teaching of Ibrahim and Moses' pages that no burden-bearer carries another's burden. This verse repeats that rule while saying each soul's gain is its own and all return to God.

The section quotes the first pages' rule that no burden-bearer carries another's burden. This verse repeats it and adds that God does not punish until sending a messenger, connecting individual responsibility with the reminder carried by revelation.

The section quotes the earlier pages' rule that no burden-bearer carries another's burden. This verse repeats it and says even a heavily burdened soul cannot have its load carried by another, clarifying the rule's force.

The section quotes the pages' rule that no burden-bearer carries another's burden. This verse repeats it and says people will be informed of their deeds when they return to God, joining individual responsibility to a final record.
The section cites the pages' statement that a person has only what they strive for. This verse supplies that specific teaching and links the written reminder to each person's own effort.

This continues the pages' account of individual effort in 53:39: “وَأَنَّ سَعْيَهُ سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ.” Its contribution is that one's effort will be seen, completing what the preceding verse says belongs to a person.

The section quotes the pages' statement that each person's effort will be seen. This verse says whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, making that disclosure concrete at the smallest scale.
This completes 99:7 with the same disclosure for an atom's weight of evil. Its contribution is the other side of the record that reveals each person's deeds.
This continues 53:40 by saying that the effort is then fully recompensed. It adds the outcome of the pages' teaching about each person's own striving.

The section quotes the pages' conclusion, “وَأَنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ الْمُنْتَهَىٰ.” This closes their sequence about individual burden and effort with its destination, rather than leaving the pages as detached maxims.

The section's 87:7 has an exception “except what Allah wills,” and its dictionary defines forgetting as no longer holding what was entrusted. This verse says Allah may cause a verse to be forgotten or replace it, making divine will govern what is retained; here the context is revelation being replaced.

The section's exception places retention under Allah's will. This verse says Allah erases what He wills and confirms what He wills, with the source-record with Him; it gives a written-decree parallel while speaking of decree rather than human memory.
The section itself cites the instruction “وَاذْكُر رَّبَّكَ إِذَا نَسِيتَ.” It supplies the remedy for the very failure named by its dictionary: when you forget, remember your Lord.

The section itself identifies Adam's forgotten charge as the first example of human forgetting. The ayah says he forgot the covenant and lacked resolve, giving a concrete instance of failing to hold what had been entrusted.

The section's dictionary form النسي names forgotten or abandoned things as well as the failure to remember. Maryam wishes she had become “نَسْيًا مَّنْسِيًّا,” a thing forgotten; this related form shifts from the section's dropped belongings to a person wishing to disappear from memory.

The section's dictionary form النسيان includes failing to retain what was entrusted. Here Moses' companion says he forgot the fish and that Satan made him forget to mention it, a concrete lapse about something carried on their journey.
The section's dictionary describes forgetting as failing to keep something in mind. Moses says “لَا تُؤَاخِذْنِي بِمَا نَسِيتُ,” acknowledging a lapse in their exchange and asking pardon.

The section's dictionary form النسيان includes losing hold of what one should remember. On the usual reading that the released prisoner forgot Joseph's request to mention him to the ruler, the verse shows a lost reminder prolonging Joseph's imprisonment; the referent of “his lord” is also read differently.

The section's dictionary distinguishes forgetting through a weak heart, inattention, or intent. This prayer asks not to be taken to task if the believers forget or err, naming ordinary failure of recall as a human limit.

The section itself cites “نَسُوا اللَّهَ فَنَسِيَهُمْ.” In context this describes hypocrites who command wrong and withhold good; Allah's answering “forgetting” is the reversal of their deliberate abandonment.

The section itself cites the warning against people who forget Allah and are made to forget themselves. Its context makes forgetting God a loss of self-knowledge, sharpening the section's distinction between held and abandoned remembrance.

The section's dictionary form النسيان is paired with remembrance and the admonition in 87:9. Here turning away from Allah's remembrance brings a constricted life, showing a consequence of abandoning that reminder.

The section's dictionary links forgetting with letting go of remembrance, and 87:16 names preference for worldly life. This verse describes a person whose heart is heedless of God's remembrance, who follows desire; it joins lost remembrance to the desire that the section contrasts with the lasting Hereafter.

The section concerns recited revelation and the audience that turns from its reminder. This verse says a hidden barrier is placed between the Prophet and those who do not believe in the Hereafter when he recites the Quran, making refusal a response to the very act of recitation.
This continues 17:45 by describing veils over their hearts and heaviness in their ears when the Prophet recites the Quran. Its contribution is the impaired reception that completes the barrier image.
The section describes words recited and gathered for the listener. This verse reports disbelievers saying, “لَا تَسْمَعُوا لِهَذَا الْقُرْآنِ,” directly staging refusal to listen to the recitation.

The section connects remembrance of God's name to prayer and the recited reminder. This verse says that when the Quran is recited to them they do not prostrate, a specific refusal at the meeting of recitation and worship.

The section itself quotes this reversal: people forgot Allah's signs when they came, and on that day they are forgotten. It gives the abandonment-and-return pattern in the dictionary and 87:7 a judgment scene.

The section's dictionary form النسيان includes leaving something behind. This verse says those deceived by worldly life forgot the meeting of that day, and today they are forgotten; it connects deliberate neglect to the passage's contrast of what lasts and what passes.

The section links admonition to remembrance. Here, after people forget what they were reminded of, they are given what they seek before sudden punishment comes; the verse shows what refusal of the reminder permits.

The section's reminder is something that brings a need back to mind. Here the wrongdoer is reminded of the Lord's signs, turns away, and forgets what his hands sent ahead; remembrance and deliberate neglect are placed in one scene.

The section's dictionary form الذكر is both remembrance and the reminder that restores it. This verse says mockery of the believers led the mockers to forget Allah's remembrance, showing how rejection of the reminder can invert the relation.

The section's dictionary form النسيان is the opposite of preserving in memory. Here the people are told they are forgotten because they forgot the meeting of this day, repeating the reciprocal reversal in a distinct judgment address.

The section's dictionary form النسيان includes leaving behind. Here those who mocked the meeting of this day are told they will be forgotten as they forgot it, a second explicit reversal of the memory relation.

The section treats remembering as the opposite of forgetting. “فَاذْكُرُونِي أَذْكُرْكُمْ” makes that relation reciprocal, adding what answered remembrance looks like in a direct address to believers.
The section says the one who fears will remember. This verse likewise places fear before recovery of attention: when the God-fearing are touched by Satan, they remember and see clearly.

The section's dictionary form أَثَرْتُ الحديث means transmitting a saying from another. This verse asks for an earlier book or “أَثَارَةٍ مِّنْ عِلْمٍ”; the latter is a remnant of knowledge, connecting transmitted words to a trace of earlier teaching.

The section's dictionary form أَثَرْتُ الحديث means transmitting another's speech. Moses' rebuke instead uses “أَثَرِ الرَّسُولِ” for a trace of the messenger: the related root shifts from transmitted words to a remaining trace, making the difference between report and residue visible.

The section's dictionary form أَثَرْتُ الحديث describes transmitting a saying from someone else. This verse says the polytheists found their fathers following a way and follow “آثَارِهِمْ”; here the related root is ancestral tracks, contrasting inherited custom with the earlier prophetic pages the section names.

The section's dictionary form أَثَرَ الحديث names something transmitted, while its نسي entry names what is left behind. This verse says God records what people send ahead and “آثَارَهُمْ,” the traces they leave, joining remembered transmission to written record.

The section's dictionary form النسي means inferior belongings left at the stations of departing travelers. Here people stand before God having “تَرَكْتُمْ مَا خَوَّلْنَاكُمْ وَرَاءَ ظُهُورِكُمْ”; the verse stages people leaving their worldly goods behind when they arrive.

The section's image moves from what is held in memory to what is written and gathered on pages. This verse says each person's record is attached to them and brought out as an open book, transferring the image of retained writing to an individual's deeds.

The section's dictionary form قرأت الشيء defines reading as gathering words together, and its pages are written records. Here the person is told “اقْرَأْ كِتَابَكَ,” to read their own open record, making the act of reading answerable to what was retained.

The section describes a mushaf as a gathering of written pages. Here the placed record leaves no small or great deed uncounted, and people find what they did present; it gives a specific picture of a record that does not drop what it holds.
The section says written pages hold what is read and remembered. “وَإِذَا الصُّحُفُ نُشِرَتْ” depicts the scrolls being opened, when their contents become available for reckoning.
The section describes sheets gathered in a book. This verse likens the rolling up of the sky to the rolling of a written scroll, extending the page image to a record being closed at the end.

The section's dictionary form النسي names what falls away after departure. This verse stages earth's vegetation flourishing, then becoming “حَصِيدًا” as though it had not flourished the day before, an explicit image of what passes and is left behind.

The section's dictionary form النسي is fallen debris left after departure. This parable says the rain-grown vegetation becomes “هَشِيمًا تَذْرُوهُ الرِّيَاحُ,” plant fragments scattered by wind; the object that was flourishing becomes what is dispersed.
The section's dictionary form النسي names fallen remnants. Here crops turn yellow and become “حُطَامًا,” giving the brief life of green growth a close image of what remains after it has passed.

The section's dictionary form النسي names discarded remnants, while 87:16–17 contrasts near life with what lasts. This verse likens worldly growth to rain-fed vegetation that withers into “حُطَامًا,” joining transient adornment to the section's image of fallen remains.

The section contrasts those who remember with those drawn toward the nearer life. This begins the sequence that in 79:38 names the person who prefers worldly life and in 79:39 gives that choice its outcome; its own contribution is the transgression preceding the choice.

The section's dictionary form تُؤْثِرُونَ means giving one thing preference. This verse uses the same root in “وَآثَرَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا,” explicitly describing the person who preferred worldly life.

The section's dictionary form تُؤْثِرُونَ means giving one thing preference, and it criticizes preferring the nearer life. This verse uses the same root for the opposite choice: the helpers prefer others over themselves even when needy, showing a reversal in what is given priority.

This follows the preference in 79:38 with the Fire as that person's abode. It makes the consequence of preferring the nearer life explicit, alongside the section's warning to those who turn from reminder.

This turns from the person preferring worldly life in 79:38 to the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains his soul from desire. It gives the counter-choice that illuminates the section's “better and more lasting” Hereafter.
This completes the counter-choice in 79:40 with the Garden as its abode. The result puts the lasting Hereafter opposite the worldly preference described in the section and 79:38.

The section's dictionary form تُؤْثِرُونَ means preferring one thing to another. This verse says the people “اسْتَحَبُّوا الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا عَلَى الْآخِرَةِ,” making the same preference explicit in its own account of those who reject faith.

The section says people prefer the nearer life although the Hereafter is better and more lasting. This verse directly asks whether they are content with worldly life over the Hereafter, then calls worldly enjoyment small beside it.

The section's 87:16–17 contrasts worldly life with what is better and enduring. This verse sets the world's enjoyment and adornment against what is with God, “خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ,” an especially close formulation of that contrast.

The section says the Hereafter is better and more lasting than the nearer life. This verse likewise calls what people are given in worldly life enjoyment and says what is with God is “خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ.”

The section's dictionary describes forgetting as letting something go and its final contrast names what remains. This verse says “مَا عِنْدَكُمْ يَنْفَدُ وَمَا عِنْدَ اللَّهِ بَاقٍ,” sharply stating what passes and what endures.
The section contrasts the nearer life with what endures. “كُلُّ مَنْ عَلَيْهَا فَانٍ” states the passing side of that boundary for all on earth.
This continues 55:26's passing of everything on earth with the enduring face of the Lord. Its contribution is the lasting counterpart, clarifying the boundary that 87:17 draws for the Hereafter.

The section contrasts the alluring nearer life with what lasts. This verse calls wealth and children an adornment of worldly life, then says abiding good works are better with the Lord in reward and hope.
The section says people prefer the nearer life. This verse says the people love “الْعَاجِلَةَ” and leave behind a heavy day, giving the same temporal preference in the language of love and neglect.

The section contrasts preferring near life with the better Hereafter. This verse describes one who desires “الْعَاجِلَةَ” and the limited worldly provision granted, giving the immediate-life choice its own consequence.
This follows the desire for the immediate in 17:18 with the person who desires the Hereafter and strives for it. It adds the positive counter-choice to the section's preference/lasting contrast.
The section's dictionary form التذكرة is that by which a need is recalled. This verse commands “وَذَكِّرْ” because reminding benefits believers, directly stating the use of the section's reminder.

The section connects fear with remembering: “سَيَذَّكَّرُ مَنْ يَخْشَىٰ.” This verse similarly says the warning benefits one who follows the Reminder and fears the Merciful, linking the audience's fear to response.

The section's 87:9 commands the Prophet to remind, and 87:10 identifies the one who fears as remembering. This verse tells the Prophet to remind by the Quran those who fear its warning, while clarifying that he is not their controller.

The section's dictionary form التذكرة is what restores something to mind. This verse calls the account a reminder for whoever has a heart or gives ear while attentive, explicitly linking reminder to receptive hearing.
The section's 87:9 gives the Prophet the command to remind. “فَذَكِّرْ إِنَّمَا أَنْتَ مُذَكِّرٌ” gives the same prophetic stance: remind, while describing him as a reminder.
This follows the command in 88:21 by saying the Prophet is not a controller over them. It marks the boundary of the reminding role that the section's command leaves unstated.

The section's dictionary form التذكرة means something used to bring a needed matter back to mind. This verse likewise names the message “تَذْكِرَةٌ,” directly connecting the Quranic reminder to that definition.

The section describes written pages as the form that carries a prophetic reminder. In this surah's context of people turning away from the reminder, each person wants to be given “صُحُفًا مُّنَشَّرَةً”; their demand for opened pages contrasts with the reminder already being addressed to them.
The section distinguishes the reminder from the person who remembers it. This verse says whoever wills may remember the reminder, making that distinction explicit.
This completes 74:54–55 by saying they do not remember unless God wills. It adds divine will as a limit on the voluntary response, echoing the section's exception in 87:7.

The section's 87:9–10 distinguishes reminder from the one who remembers. This repeated refrain says the Quran was made easy for remembrance and asks whether anyone will remember, connecting recitation's ease to response.
This repeats the Quran's being made easy for remembrance, directly joining recited revelation and recall as the section does.
This is another occurrence of the refrain that the Quran is made easy for remembrance, showing the repeated invitation to recall the revelation.
This final occurrence repeats that the Quran is made easy for remembrance, reinforcing the relation between recitation and remembered admonition.

The section's dictionary form التذكرة is what brings a matter back to mind, and its image asks how the recited word is retained. This verse calls the event a reminder and says a retaining ear “وَتَعِيَهَا أُذُنٌ وَاعِيَةٌ” holds it, joining admonition to attentive preservation.
The section treats revelation as a reminder. This verse calls the Quran “ذِكْرٌ لِلْعَالَمِينَ,” identifying it as a reminder for all worlds before describing who can choose to respond.

This follows 81:27 by saying the reminder is for whoever wills to be upright. It makes the recipient's response explicit, as the section distinguishes between people who remember and avoid the reminder.
This completes 81:28 with the limit that people do not will unless Allah wills. It echoes the section's exception while keeping the ayah's claim about human willing distinct.
The section names the reminder and the one who remembers it. This verse calls the Quran “تَذْكِرَةٌ” and says whoever wills may take a path to the Lord, spelling out the response to the reminder.
This follows the choice in 76:29 by saying people do not will unless Allah wills. It adds divine limit to the human choice, resonating with the section's “except what Allah wills.”
